q.s: A 64-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after the onset of crushing substernal chest pain with diaphoresis and nausea. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes and a 40-pack-year smoking history. Blood pressure is 84/52 mm Hg, pulse 52/min and respirations 20/min. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Jugular venous pressure is elevated to 12 cm H2O and rises further with inspiration. His ECG is shown. Aspirin and heparin are started.
o: Morphine in a small dose for pain
e: Correct. Venodilation lowers preload, and a right ventricular infarct depends on preload to fill the left heart, so nitrates can cause profound hypotension.
Wrong. An inotrope can support output in RV failure if fluids are not enough.
Wrong. An RV infarct is preload-dependent; IV fluid is the first step to support blood pressure.
Wrong. Morphine can lower preload somewhat, but nitroglycerin is the classic, more potent cause of collapse in RV infarction.
Wrong. Atropine treats symptomatic bradycardia from AV nodal ischemia and would raise heart rate and output.
Wrong. Fibrinolysis reperfuses the artery and does not itself drop preload.
Wrong. Antiplatelet therapy has no direct effect on blood pressure.
cl: Hypotension with bradycardia: the RCA also supplies the AV and SA nodes.
The lungs are clear to auscultation
The left ventricle is not failing; no pulmonary edema.
Kussmaul sign: a stiff, failing right ventricle cannot accept venous return.
q.ch: ST elevation in II, III and aVF (with V1 elevation) + hypotension + clear lungs + high JVP → right coronary occlusion with RV infarction → RV output depends on preload → venodilators such as nitroglycerin drop preload and blood pressure.
q.tr: "Right heart, right on fluids": RV infarct needs volume, so No Nitrates.
q.q2: Administration of which of the following drugs is most likely to worsen his blood pressure?

q.s: A 78-year-old man is evaluated for two episodes of light-headedness and near-syncope while climbing stairs. He also reports exertional chest tightness for 6 months. Blood pressure is 118/94 mm Hg and pulse 72/min. The carotid upstroke is weak and delayed. There is a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border that radiates to both carotid arteries, and S2 is soft. The pressure-volume loop from cardiac catheterization (dashed) is shown with a normal loop for comparison.
o: A murmur that increases with the Valsalva maneuver
Eccentric hypertrophy with a dilated left ventricle
Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with an S4
Loss of the isovolumetric contraction phase on the loop
A wide pulse pressure with bounding peripheral pulses
e: Wrong. Valsalva reduces preload and softens the murmur of aortic stenosis; HOCM gets louder.
Wrong. Eccentric hypertrophy follows volume overload, as in aortic or mitral regurgitation.
Correct. Chronic pressure overload adds sarcomeres in parallel (concentric LVH), stiffening the ventricle so atrial contraction produces an S4.
Wrong. An opening snap suggests mitral stenosis.
Wrong. That loop shape fits mitral regurgitation.
Wrong. That is aortic regurgitation; aortic stenosis narrows pulse pressure.
cl: light-headedness and near-syncope while climbing stairs
Exertional syncope: fixed outflow cannot raise output.
harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border
q.ch: Elderly + syncope, angina + parvus et tardus + crescendo-decrescendo murmur to the carotids + tall loop with high systolic pressure → aortic stenosis → chronic pressure overload → concentric LVH → stiff ventricle → S4.
q.tr: "SAD" symptoms of aortic stenosis: Syncope, Angina, Dyspnea. Pressure overload makes the wall Pumped up (concentric); volume overload makes it Puffed out (eccentric).
q.q2: Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this patient?

q.s: A 66-year-old man with COPD comes to the emergency department because of palpitations and fatigue for 2 days. He uses an albuterol inhaler several times a day. Pulse is 75/min and regular, and blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg. Thyroid function tests and electrolytes are normal. An ECG rhythm strip from lead II is shown. Rate control is achieved, but the rhythm recurs twice over the next 3 months despite medical therapy.
o: Catheter ablation of the cavotricuspid isthmus
e: Wrong. A pacemaker treats bradyarrhythmias, not a re-entrant tachyarrhythmia.
Wrong. Accessory pathways cause WPW, which shows a short PR and delta wave.
Wrong. Pulmonary vein triggers are targeted in atrial fibrillation.
Correct. Typical atrial flutter is a macro-re-entrant circuit around the tricuspid annulus in the right atrium; ablating the isthmus is curative.
Wrong. Digoxin slows AV conduction but does not eliminate the circuit.
Wrong. Adenosine is ultrashort-acting and only transiently unmasks flutter waves.
cl: Lung disease and right atrial enlargement predispose to atrial flutter.
A regular ventricular rate: fixed-ratio conduction (atrial rate 300, conducted 4:1).
recurs twice over the next 3 months despite medical therapy
Recurrent flutter is an indication for curative ablation.
q.ch: Sawtooth flutter waves at ~300/min + regular 4:1 ventricular response + COPD → typical atrial flutter → re-entry around the tricuspid annulus → ablate the cavotricuspid isthmus.
q.tr: Flutter is a "merry-go-round" in the right atrium; cut the "isthmus bridge" and the ride stops.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive treatment for this rhythm?

q.s: A 74-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after fainting while gardening. She has had two similar episodes this month. Pulse is 38/min and regular, and blood pressure is 102/60 mm Hg. The intensity of S1 varies from beat to beat. A jugular venous pulse tracing recorded at the bedside is shown.
o: Bulging of the tricuspid valve during isovolumetric contraction
Impaired right ventricular relaxation from constriction
Right atrial filling against a closed tricuspid valve
Rapid ventricular filling after tricuspid valve opening
Right atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve
e: Wrong. Tricuspid regurgitation produces a giant c-v wave in every beat.
Wrong. That is the small c wave.
Wrong. Constrictive pericarditis causes a steep y descent and Kussmaul sign.
Wrong. That is the normal v wave.
Wrong. That is the y descent.

Correct. In complete heart block the atria and ventricles beat independently; when atrial systole falls during ventricular systole, the atrium contracts against a closed valve and produces a cannon a wave.
cl: The intensity of S1 varies from beat to beat
AV dissociation: the mitral leaflets are at variable positions when systole starts.
q.ch: Syncope + regular pulse 38/min + variable S1 + intermittent huge a waves → AV dissociation in 3rd-degree heart block → atrium sometimes contracts against a closed tricuspid valve → cannon a wave.
q.tr: "Cannon a = atria Against a closed valve."
q.q2: The large wave in the second cycle is best explained by which of the following?
q.fc: Jugular venous pulse tracing over two cardiac cycles

q.s: A 38-year-old woman in opioid use disorder treatment is brought to the emergency department after collapsing at home. She takes methadone and started ondansetron 3 days ago for gastroenteritis with vomiting and diarrhea. She regained consciousness spontaneously. Serum K+ is 2.9 mEq/L and Mg2+ is 1.3 mg/dL. Her baseline ECG showed a corrected QT interval of 560 ms. While on the monitor, she has another episode; the rhythm strip is shown. She has a pulse and remains conscious after 20 seconds.
e: Wrong. Not effective for torsades and may cause hypotension.
Wrong. A class IA drug that prolongs QT.
Wrong. Not used for ventricular arrhythmias.
Wrong. Adenosine is used for AV nodal re-entrant tachycardias.
Wrong. A class III drug that prolongs QT.
Wrong. Amiodarone prolongs the QT interval and can worsen this rhythm.
Correct. This is torsades de pointes from long QT (methadone, ondansetron, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia). IV magnesium is first-line, even when serum magnesium is normal.
cl: K+ is 2.9 mEq/L and Mg2+ is 1.3 mg/dL
Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia from GI losses prolong QT.
Marked QT prolongation, the substrate for torsades.
q.ch: QT-prolonging drugs + low K+ and Mg2+ + QTc 560 ms + polymorphic VT twisting around the baseline → torsades de pointes → IV magnesium (then correct K+, stop offending drugs).
q.tr: "Torsades? Grab the Mag."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
q.fc: Lead II rhythm strip during the episode

q.s: A 32-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of progressive shortness of breath, orthopnea and one episode of blood-tinged sputum. She grew up with limited access to medical care and recalls a severe sore throat followed by painful swollen joints when she was 9 years old. Pulse is 118/min and irregularly irregular. There is a loud S1, an opening snap after S2 and a low-pitched diastolic rumble at the apex. Simultaneous pressure tracings from cardiac catheterization are shown.
o: Antibodies against streptococcal M protein cross-reacting with cardiac antigens
Myxomatous degeneration of the valve leaflets
Direct bacterial invasion of the valve endothelium
Age-related dystrophic calcification of the annulus
Deposition of immune complexes from hepatitis B infection
e: Wrong. Bicuspid valves affect the aortic valve.
Correct. Rheumatic heart disease follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis; molecular mimicry (type II hypersensitivity) damages the mitral valve, causing stenosis years later.
Wrong. Myxomatous change causes mitral valve prolapse.
Wrong. That is infective endocarditis.
Wrong. Calcific disease affects elderly patients.
Wrong. That is associated with polyarteritis nodosa.
cl: severe sore throat followed by painful swollen joints
Group A streptococcal pharyngitis followed by acute rheumatic fever (migratory polyarthritis).
Pulmonary venous hypertension from high left atrial pressure.
Atrial fibrillation from left atrial enlargement.
q.ch: Childhood strep throat + arthritis → rheumatic fever (molecular mimicry vs M protein) → mitral stenosis → LA pressure stays above LV pressure through diastole (tracing) → LA enlargement, AF, hemoptysis; pregnancy volume load unmasks it.
q.tr: Rheumatic fever is "M for M": M protein → Mitral valve.
q.q2: The primary underlying cause of this patient's valvular disease involves which of the following mechanisms?
q.fc: Simultaneous left ventricular, aortic and left atrial pressures

q.s: A 69-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction 25%) is admitted with worsening dyspnea, orthopnea and 6 kg of weight gain over 2 weeks. He has bibasilar crackles and pitting edema to the knees. Blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. His hemodynamic state is plotted as point X on the cardiac function curves shown. He receives intravenous furosemide and diureses 3 L over the next day.
e: Wrong. Removing 3 L of volume lowers filling pressure.
Wrong. Reaching the normal curve requires improved contractility, which a diuretic does not provide.
Wrong. A higher output at the same preload requires an inotrope.
Wrong. This represents higher filling pressure with lower output, a worsening state.
Correct. Diuresis lowers preload, moving him leftward along the same depressed curve; on the flat part of the curve, congestion improves with little loss of cardiac output.
cl: Reduced contractility: a depressed, flattened Frank-Starling curve.
6 kg of weight gain over 2 weeks
q.ch: Depressed curve (low EF) + high LVEDP (congestion) at point X + loop diuretic lowers preload only → move left along the same curve → point A (less congestion, output nearly unchanged).
q.tr: "Diuretics slide you along the curve; inotropes lift you to a new curve."
q.q2: Which point best represents his hemodynamic state after diuresis alone?
q.fc: Cardiac output vs left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (Frank-Starling curves)

q.s: A 58-year-old man on maintenance hemodialysis for end-stage renal disease is brought to the emergency department with generalized weakness. He missed his last two dialysis sessions. Pulse is 64/min and blood pressure is 152/90 mm Hg. Serum K+ is 7.4 mEq/L and HCO3− is 15 mEq/L. A lead II rhythm strip is shown.
e: Correct. Calcium stabilizes the cardiac membrane within minutes in hyperkalemia with ECG changes; then shift K+ into cells (insulin with glucose, albuterol) and remove it (dialysis).
Wrong. Binders remove potassium over hours and do not protect the heart now.
Wrong. These ECG changes are metabolic, not ischemic.
Wrong. He makes little urine, and diuretics act slowly.
Wrong. Insulin shifts K+ into cells but should be given with glucose and after membrane stabilization.
Wrong. Not a treatment for hyperkalemia.
Wrong. It raises potassium.
cl: missed his last two dialysis sessions
Potassium accumulates without renal or dialytic clearance.
Acidosis shifts K+ out of cells.
q.ch: ESRD + missed dialysis + K+ 7.4 + tall peaked T waves → hyperkalemia with cardiotoxicity → first stabilize the membrane with IV calcium → then shift and remove K+.
q.tr: "C BIG K Drop": Calcium, β-agonist, Insulin + Glucose, Kayexalate/binders, Dialysis. Calcium first protects the heart.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate next step in management?

q.s: A 22-year-old woman who runs marathons undergoes a pre-participation sports evaluation. She has no symptoms, takes no medications and has never fainted. Pulse is 52/min and blood pressure is 106/64 mm Hg. Physical examination is normal. A rhythm strip recorded at rest is shown. During a treadmill test, the rhythm disappears as her heart rate rises.
o: An accessory pathway bypassing the AV node
High vagal tone slowing conduction in the AV node
e: Wrong. Possible cause of AV block, but she has no exposure, rash or symptoms.
Wrong. She is asymptomatic and healthy.
Wrong. Not suggested by her history or ECG.
Wrong. WPW shows a short PR and delta wave.
Correct. Progressive PR prolongation until a dropped beat (Mobitz I/Wenckebach) is AV nodal and common in athletes; it resolves with exercise as vagal tone falls.
Wrong. Infranodal disease causes Mobitz II with sudden dropped beats and a fixed PR.
cl: Endurance training raises resting vagal tone.
Mobitz I in athletes is usually benign.
the rhythm disappears as her heart rate rises
Exercise withdraws vagal tone, so AV nodal conduction improves; infranodal block would not improve.
q.ch: Athlete + asymptomatic + PR lengthens until a P wave is not conducted + resolves with exercise → Mobitz I from high vagal tone at the AV node → reassurance.
q.tr: "Longer, longer, longer, drop: now you have a Wenckebach." Nodal = benign; Mobitz II = "the pacemaker's next."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this finding?
q.fc: Lead II rhythm strip at rest

q.s: A 67-year-old man is admitted with an inferior wall myocardial infarction treated with fibrinolysis. On hospital day 4, he develops sudden severe dyspnea and hypotension. A new loud holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex radiating to the axilla. Chest radiography shows pulmonary edema. Pressure-volume loops before (solid) and after (dashed) this event are shown.
o: Chordae tendineae of the tricuspid valve
e: Wrong. Not a complication of MI.
Wrong. That would cause tricuspid regurgitation without pulmonary edema.
Correct. It has a single blood supply (posterior descending artery, usually from the RCA), so inferior MI can rupture it 2–7 days later, causing acute mitral regurgitation.
Wrong. It has a dual supply (LAD and circumflex) and rarely ruptures.
Wrong. Free wall rupture causes tamponade with no murmur.
Wrong. Septal rupture causes a holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border with a left-to-right shunt (step-up in O2 saturation), not acute mitral regurgitation.
cl: RCA territory, which supplies the posteromedial papillary muscle.
Peak window (days 2–7) for mechanical complications as the infarct softens.
q.ch: Inferior MI (RCA) + day 4 + new apical holosystolic murmur to the axilla + pulmonary edema + loop without isovolumetric contraction → acute MR → posteromedial papillary muscle rupture.
q.tr: "Posteromedial is Poorly supplied: one artery (PDA)."
q.q2: Rupture of which of the following structures is most likely?

q.s: A 61-year-old woman is admitted to the intensive care unit with hypotension 2 days after a large anterior myocardial infarction. Her extremities are cool and mottled, urine output is 10 mL/h and she has bibasilar crackles. A pulmonary artery catheter is placed. Her hemodynamic values are shown.
e: Wrong. Hypovolemia lowers filling pressures (low PCWP and RAP).
Wrong. PE raises right-sided pressures but the wedge pressure is normal or low.
Wrong. Distributive shock with low SVR.
Wrong. Distributive shock has low SVR and usually high output.
Wrong. Neurogenic shock has low SVR and bradycardia after spinal injury.
Correct. Low cardiac index with high PCWP and high SVR is pump failure after a large MI.
q.ch: Large MI + cold, wet patient + low CI, high PCWP, high SVR, low mixed venous O2 → pump failure → cardiogenic shock.
q.tr: Shock by "pump, pipes or tank": cardiogenic = broken pump (CO ↓, PCWP ↑, SVR ↑).
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely type of shock?

q.s: A 27-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with sudden tearing chest pain radiating to his back. He is 196 cm tall with long fingers and a history of lens subluxation. Blood pressure is 168/92 mm Hg in the right arm and 128/70 mm Hg in the left arm. A soft early diastolic decrescendo murmur is heard at the left sternal border. Chest radiography shows a widened mediastinum.
e: Wrong. Causes Duchenne muscular dystrophy and dilated cardiomyopathy.
Wrong. Defective type I collagen causes osteogenesis imperfecta.
Wrong. Associated with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Correct. Marfan syndrome (FBN1, autosomal dominant) weakens the elastic scaffold of the aortic media (cystic medial degeneration), causing aortic root dilation and dissection.
Wrong. Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (type III collagen) causes arterial rupture but not lens subluxation and marfanoid habitus.
Wrong. Elastin defects cause supravalvular aortic stenosis (Williams syndrome) or cutis laxa.
cl: sudden tearing chest pain radiating to his back
Aortic regurgitation from root dilation and dissection.
q.ch: Tall + arachnodactyly + lens subluxation → Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1) → cystic medial degeneration → aortic root dilation → type A dissection (arm BP difference, widened mediastinum, AR murmur).
q.tr: "Fibrillin Fails, aorta Flails."
q.q2: A defect in which of the following proteins most likely underlies this patient's condition?

q.s: A 17-year-old boy collapses while playing basketball and recovers within 1 minute. His uncle died suddenly at age 30. A harsh systolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border. The murmur becomes louder when he stands from a squatting position. Echocardiography shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve.
e: Wrong. Venodilation lowers preload and worsens obstruction.
Correct. Raising afterload (and indirectly LV volume) widens the outflow tract and reduces the murmur of HOCM.
Wrong. Increased contractility worsens dynamic obstruction.
Wrong. Lowers preload and intensifies the murmur.
Wrong. Lowers preload, narrows the outflow tract and intensifies the murmur.
Wrong. Lowers afterload and preload, worsening obstruction.
Wrong. Lower preload worsens obstruction.
cl: His uncle died suddenly at age 30
Autosomal dominant sarcomere disease with sudden death.
louder when he stands from a squatting position
Less preload worsens dynamic outflow obstruction.
systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve
q.ch: Young athlete + syncope + family sudden death + murmur louder with less preload + asymmetric septal hypertrophy with SAM → HOCM → anything that increases LV volume or afterload (squat, handgrip) softens the murmur.
q.tr: "HOCM: fill it to quiet it." More volume or afterload = softer murmur.
q.q2: Which of the following maneuvers or interventions would decrease the intensity of this murmur?

q.s: A 31-year-old man who injects heroin is admitted with fever to 39.6°C, rigors and pleuritic chest pain for 1 week. A new holosystolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration. Chest CT shows multiple peripheral cavitating nodules in both lungs. Blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci in clusters.
o: Fungal budding yeast forming germ tubes
e: Wrong. Viridans streptococci cause subacute endocarditis of damaged left-sided valves.
Wrong. S. epidermidis infects prosthetic valves and devices.
Wrong. Candida is a less common cause.
Wrong. Enterococci cause endocarditis after GU procedures.
Wrong. Pseudomonas is an uncommon cause.
Correct. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of acute endocarditis in people who inject drugs and favors the tricuspid valve, with septic pulmonary emboli.
cl: Injection drug use, the main risk factor for right-sided endocarditis.
multiple peripheral cavitating nodules in both lungs
Septic pulmonary emboli from a tricuspid vegetation.
q.ch: IV drug use + fever + TR murmur louder with inspiration + septic lung emboli + GPC in clusters → tricuspid endocarditis → S. aureus (catalase+, coagulase+).
q.tr: "Tricuspid in Drug users: Staph aureus" — the drug user's valve is the one blood "Tries" first.
q.q2: Which of the following best identifies the most likely causative organism?

q.s: A 71-year-old man has had fatigue, night sweats and a 5-kg weight loss for 2 months. Temperature is 38.1°C. A new diastolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border, and there are painless erythematous macules on his palms. Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL with an MCV of 74 fL. Blood cultures grow Streptococcus gallolyticus. He is started on intravenous penicillin.
o: Transesophageal echocardiography alone, with no other testing
HIV testing as the main next step
e: Wrong. Enterococci, not S. gallolyticus, are linked to GU sources.
Correct. S. gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis biotype I) bacteremia or endocarditis is strongly associated with colorectal neoplasia; his iron deficiency anemia adds to the concern.
Wrong. Echo is needed for the valve, but the organism demands a search for colon cancer.
Wrong. Not specifically indicated by this organism.
Wrong. Microcytic anemia here suggests GI blood loss.
Wrong. Viridans streptococci, not S. gallolyticus, come from the mouth.
cl: night sweats and a 5-kg weight loss
Constitutional symptoms of subacute endocarditis, or malignancy.
painless erythematous macules on his palms
Microcytic, likely iron deficiency from occult GI blood loss.
q.ch: Subacute endocarditis + S. gallolyticus + iron deficiency anemia in an older adult → colonic neoplasm as the portal of entry → colonoscopy.
q.tr: "S. Bovis sits in the Bowel": bovis → colon cancer.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate additional evaluation?

q.s: An 82-year-old woman with heart failure and atrial fibrillation takes furosemide and digoxin. Two weeks ago, verapamil was added for rate control. She now has nausea, vomiting, confusion and says lights look yellow. Pulse is 46/min. Serum K+ is 6.1 mEq/L and creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL. Serum digoxin concentration is markedly elevated.
e: Correct. Life-threatening digoxin toxicity with hyperkalemia and bradyarrhythmia is treated with digoxin immune Fab.
Wrong. Verapamil raised digoxin levels and slows AV conduction.
Wrong. Digoxin has a large volume of distribution and is poorly dialyzable.
Wrong. Traditionally avoided in digoxin toxicity and does not address the cause.
Wrong. She is already hyperkalemic.
Wrong. May be used for ventricular arrhythmias but is not the definitive treatment.
cl: Verapamil decreases digoxin clearance, raising levels.
Xanthopsia, a classic sign of digoxin toxicity.
Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition shifts K+ out of cells; hyperkalemia signals severe toxicity.
q.ch: Elderly + renal impairment + verapamil interaction → digoxin accumulates → GI and visual symptoms, bradycardia, hyperkalemia → digoxin Fab.
q.tr: "Digoxin: yellow vision, high K+, slow beat — Fab to the rescue."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

q.s: A 59-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and coronary artery disease takes atorvastatin. Because of persistently high triglycerides, his physician adds a second lipid-lowering drug. Six weeks later he has diffuse muscle aches and weakness of the proximal limbs and dark urine. Serum creatine kinase is 14,000 U/L.
e: Wrong. Ezetimibe rarely causes myopathy.
Wrong. Not associated with myopathy.
Correct. Fibrates, especially gemfibrozil, inhibit statin glucuronidation and greatly increase the risk of statin myopathy and rhabdomyolysis.
Wrong. PCSK9 inhibitors are not associated with rhabdomyolysis.
Wrong. Bile acid sequestrants cause GI effects and raise triglycerides.
Wrong. Niacin can add some myopathy risk, but fibrates (gemfibrozil) are the classic culprit; niacin's hallmark effects are flushing and hyperuricemia.
cl: A statin (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor) that can cause myopathy.
Fibrates are the most effective triglyceride-lowering drugs.
q.ch: Statin + added triglyceride drug + myalgias, dark urine, very high CK → rhabdomyolysis → fibrate (gemfibrozil) interaction.
q.tr: "Statin + Fibrate = Fiber-ate your muscles."
q.q2: Which of the following drugs was most likely added?

q.s: A 16-year-old boy is evaluated after his 42-year-old father had a myocardial infarction. He has firm nodules on his Achilles tendons and a white ring at the edge of both corneas. Serum LDL cholesterol is 410 mg/dL, and triglycerides are normal. His paternal grandmother died of a heart attack at age 45.
e: Wrong. Its deficiency causes abetalipoproteinemia with very low lipids.
Wrong. Not a cause of familial hypercholesterolemia.
Wrong. Causes type I hyperchylomicronemia with pancreatitis and high triglycerides.
Correct. Familial hypercholesterolemia (autosomal dominant) results from LDL receptor defects (or apoB-100/PCSK9 mutations), causing very high LDL, tendon xanthomas and premature CAD.
Wrong. Causes dysbetalipoproteinemia with palmar xanthomas and high remnants.
Wrong. Causes chylomicronemia.
cl: firm nodules on his Achilles tendons
white ring at the edge of both corneas
Corneal arcus at a young age.
LDL cholesterol is 410 mg/dL, and triglycerides are normal
His paternal grandmother died of a heart attack at age 45
Vertical, autosomal dominant inheritance with premature CAD.
q.ch: Teen + tendon xanthomas + arcus + LDL 410 with normal TG + premature CAD in parent and grandparent → familial hypercholesterolemia (type II) → LDL receptor defect.
q.tr: "FH: Few Hooks" — too few LDL receptors to pull LDL out of blood.
q.q2: This patient's condition is most likely caused by a defect in which of the following?

q.s: A 4-year-old boy has had fever above 39°C for 6 days despite antibiotics. Examination shows bilateral nonexudative conjunctival injection, red cracked lips, a strawberry tongue, a polymorphous truncal rash, a 2-cm unilateral cervical lymph node and swelling of the hands and feet. Platelet count is 620,000/mm³ and ESR is 88 mm/h.
e: Wrong. Not associated.
Wrong. A complication of streptococcal infection.
Wrong. A late complication of rheumatic fever.
Wrong. Not a typical complication.
Correct. Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis; coronary aneurysms are the major cause of morbidity and death. IVIG and aspirin reduce the risk.
Wrong. Associated with IgA vasculitis.
cl: Mucositis (CRASH: Conjunctivitis, Rash, Adenopathy, Strawberry tongue, Hand-foot changes).
swelling of the hands and feet
q.ch: Young child + 5+ days of fever + CRASH features + thrombocytosis → Kawasaki disease (medium-vessel vasculitis) → coronary artery aneurysms → treat with IVIG and aspirin.
q.tr: "CRASH and BURN": Conjunctivitis, Rash, Adenopathy, Strawberry tongue, Hands/feet, plus fever (BURN) — and the coronaries can crash.
q.q2: Without treatment, which of the following is the most serious complication of this condition?

q.s: A 74-year-old woman has had a new right-sided headache, scalp tenderness when brushing her hair and pain in her jaw when chewing for 3 weeks. This morning she had a brief episode of blurred vision in the right eye. She also has stiffness in her shoulders and hips each morning. ESR is 96 mm/h.
o: MRI of the brain before any treatment
Temporal artery biopsy, and start therapy only if it is positive
e: Wrong. May be a steroid-sparing agent later, not initial therapy.
Wrong. Not sufficient.
Correct. Giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms risks irreversible blindness (ophthalmic artery ischemia); steroids are started at once, then biopsy is done.
Wrong. Triptans treat migraine and are contraindicated in vascular disease.
Wrong. Delays treatment.
Wrong. Biopsy should not delay treatment when vision is threatened.
cl: scalp tenderness when brushing her hair
pain in her jaw when chewing
blurred vision in the right eye
stiffness in her shoulders and hips each morning
q.ch: Elderly + new headache + scalp tenderness + jaw claudication + visual symptoms + PMR + high ESR → giant cell arteritis → treat with high-dose steroids now, biopsy after.
q.tr: "Temporal arteritis: Treat Then Test."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

q.s: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician because he becomes blue around the lips while running and then squats until he recovers. He is at the 10th percentile for weight. A harsh systolic ejection murmur is heard at the left upper sternal border. Chest radiography shows a boot-shaped heart with decreased pulmonary vascular markings.
o: Failure of the endocardial cushions to fuse
Failure of neural crest migration into the truncus
Downward displacement of the tricuspid valve
Anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum
Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to spiral
Excessive resorption of the septum primum
e: Wrong. Causes AV septal defects (common in Down syndrome).
Wrong. Causes persistent truncus arteriosus.
Wrong. Ebstein anomaly.
Correct. Tetralogy of Fallot results from anterosuperior (rostral) displacement of the infundibular septum, producing pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta, VSD and RV hypertrophy.
Wrong. Causes transposition of the great arteries.
Wrong. Causes an ostium secundum ASD.
cl: becomes blue around the lips while running
Squatting raises SVR, reducing the right-to-left shunt.
RV outflow obstruction reduces pulmonary flow.
q.ch: Cyanotic spells relieved by squatting + RVOT murmur + boot-shaped heart with oligemic lungs → tetralogy of Fallot → anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum.
q.tr: "PROVe": Pulmonary stenosis, RVH, Overriding aorta, VSD; squatting "Kinks the femorals" to push blood to the lungs.
q.q2: The embryologic event that underlies this child's condition is best described as which of the following?

q.s: A full-term newborn of a mother with poorly controlled pregestational diabetes becomes deeply cyanotic within hours of birth. Supplemental oxygen does not improve his oxygen saturation of 68%. There is no significant murmur. Chest radiography shows an "egg on a string" cardiac silhouette.
e: Wrong. Closes the ductus arteriosus, which would be fatal here.
Wrong. Not indicated.
Wrong. Does not create mixing between parallel circuits.
Wrong. Not indicated.
Wrong. Does not address the lack of mixing.
Correct. In transposition of the great arteries, the systemic and pulmonary circuits run in parallel; keeping the ductus open with PGE1 allows mixing until surgery.
cl: mother with poorly controlled pregestational diabetes
Maternal diabetes is a risk factor for transposition.
Early cyanosis as the ductus begins to close.
A fixed shunt or parallel circuits: hyperoxia test fails.
Narrow mediastinum from anteroposterior great arteries.
q.ch: Diabetic mother + profound cyanosis at birth unresponsive to O2 + egg-on-a-string heart → transposition (aorticopulmonary septum failed to spiral) → keep ductus open with PGE1.
q.tr: "Keep it open with PGE, Close it with Indomethacin."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate pharmacotherapy?

q.s: A 14-year-old girl is evaluated for short stature and absent breast development. She has a broad chest with widely spaced nipples and a webbed neck. Blood pressure is 156/88 mm Hg in the right arm; femoral pulses are weak and delayed. Chest radiography shows notching of the inferior borders of the posterior ribs.
e: Wrong. Associated with Down syndrome.
Wrong. Associated with connective tissue disease such as Marfan syndrome.
Wrong. Associated with Williams syndrome.
Wrong. Associated with lithium exposure.
Correct. Coarctation of the aorta, common in Turner syndrome (45,X), is frequently associated with a bicuspid aortic valve.
Wrong. Associated with 22q11 deletion.
q.k: Coarctation of the aorta in Turner syndrome
cl: Ovarian dysgenesis (streak ovaries) in Turner syndrome.
femoral pulses are weak and delayed
notching of the inferior borders of the posterior ribs
q.ch: Short stature + amenorrhea + webbed neck → Turner syndrome → coarctation (arm hypertension, weak femorals, rib notching) → associated bicuspid aortic valve.
q.tr: Turner's "3 C's of the heart": Coarctation, bicuspid (Cusp) valve, and dissection risk (Calamity).
q.q2: Which of the following cardiac abnormalities is most commonly associated with this patient's vascular lesion?

q.s: A 2-month-old girl is evaluated for poor feeding and failure to thrive. Her mother had a fever and rash during the first trimester and was not vaccinated. The infant has bilateral cataracts and failed her newborn hearing screen. A continuous machine-like murmur is heard below the left clavicle. Peripheral pulses are bounding.
e: Wrong. Keeps the ductus open.
Correct. A patent ductus arteriosus (congenital rubella) is closed by NSAIDs such as indomethacin or ibuprofen, which lower prostaglandin E2.
Wrong. Oxygen promotes closure at birth but is not an effective therapy for a persistent PDA.
Wrong. Not used.
Wrong. May treat congestion but does not close the ductus.
Wrong. Does not close the ductus.
cl: fever and rash during the first trimester
Congenital rubella triad: cataracts, deafness, PDA.
q.ch: First-trimester maternal rash + cataracts + deafness + continuous machine murmur + bounding pulses → congenital rubella with PDA → close with indomethacin.
q.tr: Rubella's "Cats, Ears, Ducts": Cataracts, deafness, ductus.
q.q2: Which of the following is most likely to close this infant's cardiac defect without surgery?

q.s: A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a stab wound to the left parasternal chest. Blood pressure is 76/58 mm Hg and pulse 132/min. His neck veins are distended and heart sounds are distant. His systolic blood pressure falls by 18 mm Hg during inspiration. The ECG shows alternating amplitude of the QRS complexes.
o: Increased right ventricular filling during inspiration bows the septum into the left ventricle, reducing LV filling
Inspiration reduces venous return to the right heart
e: Correct. With a fixed pericardial volume, extra RV filling shifts the septum left and lowers LV stroke volume (pulsus paradoxus).
Wrong. Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart.
Wrong. Hypovolemia flattens neck veins.
Wrong. Would cause absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation.
Wrong. Not the mechanism.
Wrong. Not the mechanism.
cl: stab wound to the left parasternal chest
Penetrating injury to the anterior heart (RV).
neck veins are distended and heart sounds are distant
falls by 18 mm Hg during inspiration
alternating amplitude of the QRS complexes
Electrical alternans: heart swinging in fluid.
q.ch: Penetrating chest trauma + hypotension, JVD, muffled sounds + pulsus paradoxus + electrical alternans → tamponade → equalized pressures; inspiration fills the RV, septum bows into LV → lower LV output.
q.tr: Beck's triad = "3 D's": Distended veins, Distant heart sounds, Decreased pressure.
q.q2: The inspiratory fall in blood pressure is best explained by which of the following?

q.s: A 52-year-old man has had progressive leg swelling, abdominal distension and fatigue for 6 months. He received mediastinal radiation for Hodgkin lymphoma 20 years ago. His jugular venous pressure is 16 cm H2O and rises with inspiration. An early diastolic sound is heard just after S2. Chest radiography shows a calcified rim around the heart. Ejection fraction is normal.
e: Wrong. JVP would not be elevated.
Wrong. Would cause a diastolic rumble, not a knock and pericardial calcification.
Wrong. Tamponade causes pulsus paradoxus but usually not Kussmaul sign, and there is no knock.
Wrong. Similar physiology, but a calcified pericardium and knock point to constriction.
Correct. A thick, calcified pericardium after radiation limits diastolic filling, causing Kussmaul sign and a pericardial knock with normal systolic function.
Wrong. EF would be reduced.
cl: A common cause of constrictive pericarditis (also TB, prior surgery).
early diastolic sound is heard just after S2
Pericardial knock: abrupt halt of ventricular filling.
q.ch: Prior radiation + right-sided congestion + Kussmaul sign + pericardial knock + calcified pericardium + normal EF → constrictive pericarditis.
q.tr: Constriction "Knocks and Kussmauls"; tamponade is "Paradoxical."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 70-year-old man becomes light-headed when he stands up quickly from bed. Within seconds his heart rate rises and the light-headedness resolves. A physiology student models this response.
o: Decreased afferent firing in the glossopharyngeal nerve from the carotid sinus
Release of ANP from the atria
Increased firing of carotid sinus baroreceptors
Increased firing of aortic arch receptors via CN X
Increased vagal outflow to the SA node
e: Correct. Standing pools blood in the legs, lowering arterial pressure; less stretch reduces carotid sinus firing via CN IX, so the medulla raises sympathetic and lowers vagal outflow.
Wrong. Sympathetic outflow increases.
Wrong. Not the immediate reflex response.
Wrong. Lower arterial pressure decreases stretch and firing.
Wrong. Aortic arch firing also decreases.
Wrong. Vagal outflow decreases.
cl: Venous pooling lowers preload and arterial pressure.
Within seconds his heart rate rises
A rapid neural reflex, the baroreflex.
q.ch: Standing → venous pooling → ↓ arterial pressure → ↓ carotid sinus stretch → ↓ CN IX afferent firing → medulla ↑ sympathetic, ↓ parasympathetic → ↑ HR, contractility and vasoconstriction.
q.tr: "Low pressure, low firing": baroreceptors fire in proportion to stretch.
q.q2: Immediately after he stands, which of the following changes occurs first in this reflex?

q.s: A 58-year-old man with alcohol use disorder has dyspnea on exertion and orthopnea. The apical impulse is displaced laterally. A low-pitched sound is heard at the apex shortly after S2 with the bell, with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 25%.
o: Opening of a stenotic mitral valve
Atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle
e: Wrong. Systolic events produce ejection clicks and murmurs.
Wrong. That produces an opening snap.
Correct. S3 occurs in early diastole as blood rushes into a dilated, volume-overloaded ventricle.
Wrong. No filling occurs then.
Wrong. That is S4, just before S1.
Wrong. Valves are closed and no filling occurs.
q.ch: Alcohol + dilated LV with low EF + low-pitched early diastolic apical sound → S3 → rapid early filling of a dilated ventricle.
q.tr: S3 sounds like "Ken-tuc-KY" (slosh after S2); S4 sounds like "TEN-nes-see" (before S1).
q.q2: This extra heart sound is produced during which phase of the cardiac cycle?

q.s: A 52-year-old woman with hypertension and diabetic nephropathy started a new antihypertensive drug 3 weeks ago. She now has sudden swelling of her lips and tongue without urticaria or itching. She has no known allergies.
e: Wrong. Hereditary angioedema; ACE inhibitors are contraindicated there.
Wrong. ACE inhibitors lower angiotensin II.
Wrong. ACE inhibitor angioedema is not IgE-mediated; there is no urticaria.
Wrong. A real side effect, but it does not cause angioedema.
Wrong. Not the mechanism.
Correct. ACE (kininase II) degrades bradykinin; ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin, causing angioedema and cough.
cl: ACE inhibitors are first-line for diabetic kidney disease.
started a new antihypertensive drug 3 weeks ago
Timing points to a drug reaction.
q.ch: Diabetic nephropathy → ACE inhibitor → ↓ bradykinin breakdown → angioedema without urticaria → stop ACEi; an ARB is usually a reasonable alternative.
q.tr: ACE inhibitor side effects "CATCHH": Cough, Angioedema, Teratogen, Creatinine rise, Hyperkalemia, Hypotension.
q.q2: Which of the following best explains this adverse reaction?

q.s: A 64-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction takes lisinopril, carvedilol and furosemide. Spironolactone is added and his symptoms improve. Four months later he reports tender enlargement of both breasts.
e: Wrong. Not the cause.
Correct. Eplerenone is a selective mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist without spironolactone's antiandrogenic effect, and it keeps the mortality benefit.
Wrong. Loses the mortality benefit of aldosterone antagonism.
Wrong. Not appropriate.
Wrong. Digoxin can rarely cause gynecomastia and does not solve the problem.
Wrong. β-blockers reduce mortality in HFrEF and do not cause gynecomastia.
cl: heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
Aldosterone antagonists reduce mortality in HFrEF.
q.ch: HFrEF + spironolactone + gynecomastia (antiandrogen effect) → switch to the selective agent eplerenone.
q.tr: "Eplerenone: Exactly aldosterone, Excludes androgens."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate change in therapy?

q.s: A 61-year-old man had an anterior myocardial infarction 3 months ago and has a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35%. He now has frequent premature ventricular contractions on Holter monitoring and asks about a drug to suppress them. His physician recalls a large trial in which one drug class increased mortality in post-MI patients.
e: Wrong. Secondary prevention after MI.
Wrong. β-blockers reduce mortality after MI.
Wrong. Improves remodeling after MI.
Correct. Class IC drugs increased mortality after MI (CAST trial) and are contraindicated in structural or ischemic heart disease because they are proarrhythmic.
Wrong. Reduces cardiovascular events.
Wrong. Can be used in structural heart disease.
cl: The CAST trial result for class IC drugs.
q.ch: Prior MI + low EF + PVCs → class IC (flecainide, propafenone) are proarrhythmic in scarred myocardium → contraindicated.
q.tr: "IC = I Can't use it after an infarct."
q.q2: Which of the following drugs should be avoided in this patient?

q.s: A 66-year-old man has taken a drug for recurrent ventricular tachycardia for 2 years. He now has progressive dyspnea and a dry cough. Pulmonary function testing shows a restrictive pattern with reduced diffusing capacity. He also has blue-gray discoloration of sun-exposed skin, corneal microdeposits and an elevated TSH.
e: Correct. Amiodarone causes pulmonary fibrosis, thyroid dysfunction, blue-gray skin, corneal deposits and hepatotoxicity; monitor PFTs, TFTs and LFTs.
Wrong. Given IV; causes CNS toxicity.
Wrong. Mainly QT prolongation.
Wrong. Causes cinchonism and diarrhea.
Wrong. Causes drug-induced lupus.
Wrong. Causes QT prolongation but not this multisystem toxicity.
cl: Amiodarone is used for ventricular arrhythmias.
restrictive pattern with reduced diffusing capacity
q.ch: Antiarrhythmic for VT + pulmonary fibrosis + blue-gray skin + corneal deposits + thyroid dysfunction → amiodarone.
q.tr: Amiodarone affects the organs of a lab panel: "check PFTs, LFTs, TFTs."
q.q2: Which drug most likely caused these findings?

q.s: A 58-year-old woman has resistant hypertension treated with several drugs, including one that causes direct arteriolar vasodilation. She now has fever, joint pain in her hands and a pleural effusion. Antinuclear antibodies and antihistone antibodies are positive; anti-dsDNA antibodies are negative.
e: Wrong. Relevant to azathioprine.
Wrong. Relevant to oxidant drugs causing hemolysis.
Correct. Hydralazine (like procainamide and isoniazid) is metabolized by N-acetyltransferase; slow acetylators accumulate the drug and develop drug-induced lupus.
Wrong. Slow acetylators are at higher risk.
Wrong. Allopurinol hypersensitivity.
Wrong. Not relevant.
cl: joint pain in her hands and a pleural effusion
q.ch: Hydralazine + lupus-like syndrome + antihistone positive, anti-dsDNA negative → drug-induced lupus → slow acetylators at risk.
q.tr: Drug-induced lupus "SHIPP-E": Sulfonamides, Hydralazine, Isoniazid, Procainamide, Phenytoin, Etanercept. Slow acetylators are slow to clear them.
q.q2: Which of the following increases her risk of this adverse effect?

q.s: A 49-year-old man with a hypertensive emergency (blood pressure 240/140 mm Hg with papilledema) is treated with a continuous intravenous infusion for 3 days at a high dose. He becomes confused and develops lactic acidosis. Arterial blood gas shows an unusually high venous oxygen saturation.
e: Wrong. Opioid antagonist.
Wrong. Benzodiazepine antagonist.
Wrong. Treats methemoglobinemia.
Wrong. Methanol and ethylene glycol.

Correct. Prolonged nitroprusside releases cyanide, which blocks cytochrome oxidase (lactic acidosis, high venous O2). Thiosulfate donates sulfur to convert cyanide to thiocyanate; hydroxocobalamin is an alternative.
Wrong. Acetaminophen.
cl: continuous intravenous infusion for 3 days at a high dose
q.ch: Hypertensive emergency + prolonged nitroprusside → cyanide release → blocked complex IV → lactic acidosis, high venous O2, confusion → sodium thiosulfate.
q.tr: "Nitroprusside gives you CN; Thiosulfate Takes it away."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate antidote?

q.s: A 24-year-old man has had progressive dyspnea and fatigue for 3 weeks. Two weeks before onset, he had a febrile illness with sore throat and diarrhea. Troponin is elevated, but coronary angiography is normal. Echocardiography shows global left ventricular hypokinesis. Endomyocardial biopsy shows a lymphocytic infiltrate with myocyte necrosis.
o: Flagellated protozoan transmitted by the reduviid bug
e: Wrong. Trypanosoma cruzi causes Chagas cardiomyopathy, typically with megacolon or megaesophagus and travel history.
Correct. Coxsackie B virus, a picornavirus (enterovirus), is the most common cause of viral myocarditis and can lead to dilated cardiomyopathy.
Wrong. Not the typical cause.
Wrong. Herpesviruses are an uncommon cause.
Wrong. Influenza and others are less common causes.
Wrong. Lyme carditis usually causes AV block.
cl: febrile illness with sore throat and diarrhea
q.ch: Young adult + preceding viral illness + heart failure with troponin rise and normal coronaries + lymphocytic myocarditis → Coxsackie B (picornavirus: nonenveloped +ssRNA).
q.tr: "Coxsackie B = Bad heart" (B for Beats); picornaviruses are "PERCH": Polio, Echo, Rhino, Coxsackie, Hep A.
q.q2: The most likely causative agent has which of the following characteristics?

q.s: A 46-year-old woman has episodes of dizziness and shortness of breath that occur when she leans forward or stands. She also has low-grade fevers, weight loss and arthralgias. An early diastolic low-pitched sound is heard at the apex, and its timing changes with position. ESR and serum IL-6 are elevated. Echocardiography shows a pedunculated mass attached to the interatrial septum.
e: Wrong. Most common cardiac tumor in children, associated with tuberous sclerosis.
Wrong. Usually on valves.
Wrong. No mass, and symptoms are not positional.

Correct. The most common primary cardiac tumor in adults, usually in the left atrium attached to the septum; it causes positional "ball-valve" obstruction, a tumor plop and constitutional symptoms from IL-6.
Wrong. Metastases are more common overall but are not pedunculated septal masses with this picture.
Wrong. Not pedunculated on the septum with constitutional symptoms.
cl: when she leans forward or stands
Positional obstruction of the mitral orifice.
low-grade fevers, weight loss and arthralgias
pedunculated mass attached to the interatrial septum
q.ch: Positional syncope or dyspnea + tumor plop + IL-6 constitutional symptoms + pedunculated septal LA mass → atrial myxoma.
q.tr: "Myxoma Mostly in the Mitral side (left atrium)"; Rhabdomyoma in Rookies (children).
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 70-year-old man had an anterior wall myocardial infarction 5 days ago treated medically because he arrived late. He suddenly becomes unresponsive with a blood pressure of 60/40 mm Hg. Neck veins are distended and heart sounds are muffled. There is no new murmur. The ECG shows sinus rhythm.
o: Neutrophil infiltration as the predominant cell
e: Wrong. Complete by about 2 months.
Wrong. Typical of early reperfusion injury.
Wrong. Peaks at 1–3 days.
Wrong. Seen at 4–24 hours.
Wrong. Sarcoidosis.
Correct. At 3–14 days, macrophages remove necrotic tissue; the softened wall is most prone to free wall rupture (here, causing tamponade).
q.k: Myocardial infarction timeline and free wall rupture
cl: The 3–14 day window of macrophage-mediated softening.
treated medically because he arrived late
Neck veins are distended and heart sounds are muffled
Tamponade from ventricular free wall rupture.
Argues against papillary muscle or septal rupture.
q.ch: MI day 5 without reperfusion + sudden shock with tamponade signs and no murmur → free wall rupture → myocardium at 3–14 days shows macrophages and early granulation tissue.
q.tr: MI timeline "Neutrophils at 1–3, Macrophages at 3–14, Scar by 2 months"; rupture peaks when Macrophages Munch the wall.
q.q2: Which of the following histologic findings would be expected in the infarcted myocardium at this time?

q.s: A 55-year-old man has crushing chest pain for 45 minutes. ECG shows ST elevation in leads V1 through V4. Emergency angiography shows complete occlusion of one artery, which is opened with a stent.
o: The lateral and posterior left ventricle
The posterior third of the interventricular septum and inferior wall
The AV node in a right-dominant heart
The anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum and the anterior left ventricle
The SA node and right atrium in most people
e: Wrong. Right marginal branches of the RCA.
Wrong. Left circumflex.
Wrong. Supplied by the posterior descending artery.
Wrong. Supplied by the RCA.
Correct. The LAD supplies the anterior LV, anterior two-thirds of the septum, anterolateral papillary muscle and LV apex; anteroseptal ST elevation (V1–V4) points to it.
Wrong. Usually the RCA.
cl: ST elevation in leads V1 through V4
q.ch: ST elevation V1–V4 → anteroseptal/anterior MI → LAD territory (anterior 2/3 of septum, anterior LV, apex).
q.tr: ECG "leads to arteries": V1–V2 septal, V3–V4 anterior = LAD; II, III, aVF = RCA; I, aVL, V5–V6 = circumflex.
q.q2: Which of the following regions of the heart is supplied by the occluded artery?

q.s: A 79-year-old man has progressive exertional dyspnea, bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome and leg edema. ECG shows low QRS voltage, but echocardiography shows thick ventricular walls with a granular, "sparkling" appearance and impaired diastolic filling. Ejection fraction is 55%. Endomyocardial biopsy shows deposits with apple-green birefringence under polarized light after Congo red staining.
o: Immunoglobulin light chains in multiple myeloma
e: Correct. Senile systemic (wild-type ATTR) amyloidosis affects elderly men, causing restrictive cardiomyopathy and carpal tunnel syndrome.
Wrong. Dialysis-related amyloidosis affects joints.
Wrong. AA amyloidosis follows chronic inflammation and usually affects the kidneys.
Wrong. Type 2 diabetes.
Wrong. AL amyloidosis is possible, but age, carpal tunnel and isolated cardiac disease favor wild-type transthyretin.
Wrong. Alzheimer disease and cerebral amyloid angiopathy.
cl: Amyloid deposition in the carpal ligament, often preceding cardiac disease in ATTR.
low QRS voltage, but echocardiography shows thick ventricular walls
The classic mismatch: infiltration, not true hypertrophy.
q.ch: Elderly man + carpal tunnel + low-voltage ECG with thick walls + restrictive filling + Congo red apple-green → wild-type transthyretin amyloidosis.
q.tr: "Thick walls, thin voltage = amyloid"; in the elderly, think "TTR: Too Terribly old for Rhythm."
q.q2: Which of the following proteins most likely forms these deposits?

q.s: A 28-year-old woman has had headaches for 3 months. Blood pressure is 176/104 mm Hg on several visits. She takes no medications and has no family history of hypertension. A bruit is heard in the right upper abdomen. Plasma renin activity and aldosterone are both elevated. Serum K+ is 3.2 mEq/L. Angiography of the right renal artery shows a "string of beads" appearance.
e: Wrong. Renin would be suppressed.
Wrong. Typical in older patients with vascular risk factors; affects the ostium.
Wrong. Arm-leg BP difference and rib notching.
Wrong. A granulomatous vasculitis with constitutional symptoms and weak upper-extremity pulses.
Wrong. Episodic symptoms with high metanephrines.

Correct. A noninflammatory, nonatherosclerotic arterial disease of young women that causes renal artery stenosis with a "string of beads" pattern and renin-mediated (secondary hyperaldosteronism) hypertension.
cl: Young women are typical for fibromuscular dysplasia.
bruit is heard in the right upper abdomen
Plasma renin activity and aldosterone are both elevated
Classic angiographic sign of fibromuscular dysplasia.
q.ch: Young woman + severe hypertension + abdominal bruit + high renin and aldosterone + hypokalemia + string-of-beads renal artery → fibromuscular dysplasia → renovascular hypertension.
q.tr: "Beads on a young lady's string" = fibromuscular dysplasia.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her hypertension?
